summary: Describes the S/KEY One-Time Password system released by Bellcore. Each login uses a password that works once, so a captured password cannot be reused. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: S/KEY creates a sequence of passwords that can each be used once. A captured password cannot be used to calculate the next one without reversing the hash function.

questions: how does s/key one-time password work
how does s/key protect against replay attacks
subtitle: A one-time password method that prevents a captured login password from being reused.

tldr.problem: An eavesdropper can capture a reusable login password and try it again later in a replay attack.
tldr.mechanism: The client applies a hash repeatedly to a secret pass-phrase combined with a server-provided seed. Each login uses a value one hash step earlier in the sequence, and the host verifies it by hashing once.
tldr.outcome: S/KEY keeps the secret pass-phrase off the network and avoids storing secret information on the host. It does not stop active attacks or protect private data from an eavesdropper.

today: RFC 1760 is an Informational memo describing the S/KEY system released for public use. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Threat and the Protection
sections.content:
S/KEY addresses replay attacks, where someone listens to a network login and later reuses the captured user name and password. The user's secret pass-phrase never crosses the network, including during login or commands that require authentication.

The host does not need to store secret information. The RFC limits the protection: S/KEY addresses external passive attacks on authentication, but not active attackers who can change traffic, insider attacks or eavesdropping on private information.
sections.plainLanguage: A password that works only once cannot be replayed at a later login. S/KEY protects the authentication exchange, but it does not hide other data sent over the network.

sections.title: Hashing the Secret
sections.content:
A secure hash is easy to compute in one direction and computationally infeasible to reverse. S/KEY uses MD4 and folds its 128-bit output to 64 bits with exclusive-or. The RFC says MD4 was retained because many client programs already used it; clients and hosts must use the same hash function.

The user's pass-phrase is combined with a non-secret seed from the server, then hashed and reduced to 64 bits. The seed allows the same pass-phrase to be used on different machines with different seeds. The pass-phrase should be more than eight characters, and the seed should be alphanumeric without blanks.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash turns information into a value that is difficult to reverse. S/KEY combines the pass-phrase with a seed before hashing, so the pass-phrase itself is not sent to the host.

sections.title: Generating the Password Sequence
sections.content:
After the preparatory step creates value S, the client hashes S the user-selected number of times to produce the first password. The next password uses one fewer hash operation, and each later password continues down that sequence. A person who sees one password cannot calculate the next without reversing the hash.

The resulting password is 64 bits. For manual entry, the RFC represents it as six short English words from a shared dictionary of 2048 words. All hosts and calculators need the same dictionary to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: The client makes a sequence by applying the hash a chosen number of times, then one fewer time for each later password. Each password is a single-use value, represented as six dictionary words for manual entry.

sections.title: Challenge and Password Format
sections.content:
The host gives the client a challenge containing the current sequence number and seed. Its format is s/key sequence_integer seed, with the three parts separated by single spaces and the challenge ended by a blank or newline.

The client uses the challenge and secret pass-phrase to compute the password. A calculator may display it, insert it into an input stream or provide it for manual entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The host sends the sequence number and seed that the client needs. The client combines them with the secret pass-phrase to produce the password for this login.

sections.title: Checking and Resetting the Sequence
sections.content:
For each user, the host stores the last successful one-time password, or an initial value set up with the keyinit command. To check a login, the host hashes the submitted password once and compares the result with its stored value. If they match, login succeeds and the submitted password becomes the stored value.

The sequence eventually runs out because the number of hash operations decreases with use. The user must reinitialize the system with a new pass-phrase, iteration count or seed before that happens.
sections.plainLanguage: The host checks a submitted password by hashing it once and comparing the result with its saved value. Before the sequence runs out, the user resets it with new S/KEY parameters.
